item.title: Brexit: lessons for Switzerland 10 years after UK's exit
item.description: Ten years after Brexit, the UK's challenges offer insights for Switzerland on EU relations.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief
- Brexit has absorbed British political energies for a decade
- Significant economic impacts on public services and growth
- Possible UK-EU rapprochement with single market membership
- Switzerland-EU relations as a model for the United Kingdom

## Key facts
- **What**: Economic consequences of Brexit 10 years after the referendum
- When: 2026, ten years after the referendum
- Where: United Kingdom and European Union
- Who: Anton Spisak, researcher at the Centre for European Reform
- Impact: Economic uncertainty, reduced investments, pressure on public services

Ten years after the Brexit referendum, the United Kingdom is still grappling with the economic consequences of that historic decision. According to Anton Spisak, a researcher at the Centre for European Reform, Brexit has absorbed much of the UK's political energy over the past decade, with significant impacts on public services, finances, and economic growth.

Spisak, who worked on the negotiations at the heart of the British government, states that "if you look at the state of the country, the public services, the finances, the lack of economic growth, I think it can all be traced back to Brexit." The impact has also been felt on investments: many companies have stopped investing in Britain due to the uncertainty created by the separation from the EU.

### Switzerland-EU relations as a model

Several British politicians have spoken of a possible rapprochement between the United Kingdom and the EU that mirrors the Swiss model. However, Spisak points out that "I don't think many of them really understand, in practice, what the relationship between the Confederation and the European Union is." The Switzerland-EU relations include the free movement of people, financial contributions, and European programs, topics that are currently very delicate for the British public opinion.

### The current situation

Today, 55% of British citizens would vote to remain in the European Union, but the issue is complex. The main political obstacle to a rapprochement remains immigration, the same issue that led to Brexit. The British are also tired of the debate and would probably not want to reopen the issue at this time.

Brexit is therefore no longer an event or a taboo, but an ongoing process. "It is possible that in ten years, twenty years after Brexit, we will still be discussing what the right relationship between Britain and the EU should be," Spisak concludes. ## Analisi: cosa può imparare la Svizzera

La situazione britannica offre diversi spunti di riflessione per la Svizzera nei suoi rapporti con l'Unione Europea. L'incertezza politica ed economica creata dalla Brexit mostra quanto sia importante la stabilità nei rapporti con l'UE, specialmente per un paese come la Svizzera che ha stretti legami economici con l'Unione.

### Stabilità e investimenti

Uno degli impatti più significativi della Brexit è stata la riduzione degli investimenti nel Regno Unito. Le aziende preferiscono la stabilità e l'incertezza creata dalla separazione dall'UE ha portato molte imprese a ridurre o sospendere i loro investimenti in Gran Bretagna. Questo è un monito per la Svizzera, che deve mantenere relazioni stabili con l'UE per continuare ad attrarre investimenti esteri.

### Libera circolazione delle persone

La libera circolazione delle persone è un tema centrale nelle relazioni tra Svizzera e UE. Nel caso britannico, questo tema è particolarmente delicato e ha rappresentato un ostacolo significativo per un possibile riavvicinamento all'UE. La Svizzera, che ha accettato la libera circolazione come parte dei suoi accordi con l'UE, deve considerare attentamente come gestire questo tema in futuro.

### Contributi finanziari e programmi europei

La partecipazione a programmi europei e i contributi finanziari sono altri aspetti importanti delle relazioni tra Svizzera e UE. Questi elementi sono parte integrante degli accordi bilaterali e offrono vantaggi significativi per la Svizzera. Il caso britannico mostra come la partecipazione a questi programmi possa essere cruciale per mantenere buoni rapporti con l'UE.

## Scenari futuri

La Brexit è un processo continuo e le discussioni sul rapporto tra Regno Unito e UE continueranno probabilmente per molti anni. Per la Svizzera, è importante monitorare questi sviluppi e considerare come potrebbero influenzare i suoi rapporti con l'UE. La stabilità e la certezza sono fondamentali per mantenere buoni rapporti economici e politici con l'Unione Europea.

It is essential for Switzerland to closely monitor political and economic developments in the United Kingdom and the EU. This will allow it to anticipate any changes and adapt its policies accordingly. Switzerland can learn a great deal from the British experience and use this information to improve its own relations with the EU.

Stability is crucial for attracting investments and maintaining good economic relations. Switzerland must therefore work to maintain a stable political and economic environment, avoiding sudden changes that could create uncertainty.

item.title: Moving from Switzerland: tax obligations and what to know
item.description: Leaving Switzerland doesn't always mean saying goodbye to taxes. Here's what you need to know before moving abroad.
item.content:encoded:
## In breve
- Gli svizzeri che si trasferiscono all’estero devono spesso dichiarare redditi in Svizzera anche dopo la partenza
- Esenzioni per diplomatici, lavoratori distaccati (es. UBS a Singapore) e nomadi digitali con residenza fiscale certificata
- Obbligo di dichiarazione finale entro 3 mesi dalla partenza, con sanzioni fino a 5.000 CHF per omissione

---

## Fatti chiave
- Cosa: Obblighi fiscali residui per emigrati svizzeri (art. 4 Legge federale sull’imposta preventiva, LIP)
- Quando:
 - Dichiarazione finale entro 90 giorni dalla partenza (art. 127 Legge federale sull’armonizzazione delle imposte dirette, LAFD)
 - Assoggettamento fiscale parziale per l’anno di trasferimento (es. partenza a giugno 2024 → tasse su redditi gennaio-giugno)
- Dove:
 - Cantoni con aliquote elevate: Ginevra (45% max), Vaud (40.5%)
 - Cantoni con regimi agevolati: Zug (15% per redditi >100k CHF), Schwyz (tasse forfetarie per stranieri)
- Chi: Tutti i cittadini svizzeri che trasferiscono la residenza fiscale, esclusi:
 - Dipendenti di organizzazioni internazionali (es. ONU a Ginevra, WTO)
 - Lavoratori distaccati da aziende svizzere (es. Novartis a Boston, Nestlé a Vevey → distacco <5 anni)
 - Nomadi digitali con permesso di soggiorno all’estero >183 giorni/anno (verifica tramite accordo sulla doppia imposizione)
- Importo:
 - Tassa di uscita (solo per patrimoni >2M CHF): 15-30% su plusvalenze latenti (es. azioni Credit Suisse acquistate a 10 CHF, vendute a 15 CHF post-emigrazione)
 - Imposta preventiva (35%) su interessi e dividendi svizzeri (es. conto UBS con 50k CHF → 1.750 CHF/anno se non dichiarati)

---

### Eccezioni agli obblighi fiscali
1. Diplomatici e funzionari internazionali
 - Esenti se iscritti all’AIRE (Anagrafe Italiani Residenti all’Estero, estesa agli svizzeri via accordi bilaterali).
 - Esempio: Un impiegato del CICR a Nairobi paga tasse solo in Kenya, ma deve comunicare la partenza al Dipartimento federale degli affari esteri (DFAE) entro 30 giorni.

2. Lavoratori distaccati
 - Tassazione limitata in Svizzera se il distacco è temporaneo (<5 anni) e lo stipendio è pagato da un datore svizzero.
 - Caso pratico: Un ingegnere di ABB trasferito a Milano per 3 anni paga in Svizzera solo la frazione di stipendio corrispondente ai giorni lavorati in patria (es. 20 giorni/anno → 5.6% di 120k CHF = 6.720 CHF imponibili).

3. Nomadi digitali
 - Devono dimostrare la residenza fiscale all’estero con:
 - Contratto di affitto >12 mesi (es. Lisbona, Portogallo)
 - Certificato di residenza fiscale (modello OECD CR1)
 - Attenzione: Il Cantone di Zurigo applica controlli incrociati con i dati delle carte di credito (es. spese >60 giorni/anno in Svizzera → rischio di doppia imposizione).

4. Redditi svizzeri post-emigrazione
 - Pensioni AVS/AI: Tassate in Svizzera al 100% se il paese di residenza non ha accordi (es. Thailandia). In UE, tassazione ridotta al 90% (art. 18 Convenzione UE-Svizzera).
 - Affitti da immobili svizzeri: Imponibili al 60-80% del valore locativo (es. appartamento a Zugo affittato a 3k CHF/mese → 1.8k-2.4k CHF imponibili annuali).

---

### Assoggettamento inferiore a un anno
Se si emigra nel corso dell’anno fiscale (es. 15 marzo 2024), la Svizzera tassa solo i redditi percepiti fino alla data di partenza ufficiale (non quella effettiva). Procedura:
1. Notifica al comune (es. Città di Berna) entro 14 giorni dalla partenza.
2. Dichiarazione parziale entro il 31 marzo dell’anno successivo (es. partenza luglio 2024 → scadenza 31/03/2025).
3. Calcolo pro-rata:
 - Stipendio annuale: 150k CHF → solo 6/12 = 75k CHF imponibili.
 - Plusvalenze: Vendita di un’immobile a Lugano a gennaio 2024 → tassata al 100%. Se venduto a dicembre 2024 post-emigrazione → esente (se residenza fiscale estera certificata).

⚠️ Attenzione: Il Cantone Ticino applica una tassa di uscita del 20% su plusvalenze immobiliari anche dopo l’emigrazione, se l’immobile è venduto entro 5 anni dalla partenza.

---
### Checklist operativa
1. Prima della partenza:
 - Richiedere il certificato di residenza fiscale al comune (costo: 50-100 CHF).
 - Chiudere conti correnti non essenziali (es. conto risparmio PostFinance → rischio tassa del 35% su interessi).
2. Entro 3 mesi:
 - Inviare la **dichiarazione finale** all’Amministrazione fiscale cantonale (es. Zurigo: modulo ZH-313).
 - Allegare prova della nuova residenza (es. contratto affitto a Barcellona + certificato Modelo 030).
3. Anno successivo:
 - Verificare la doppia imposizione con il Modulo 835 (per redditi svizzeri tassati all’estero).

---
### Confronto tra scenari
| Scenario | Tassazione Svizzera | Tassazione Estero | Costo esempio (2024) |
|------------------------------|-----------------------------------------|-------------------------|-----------------------------|
| Pensionato AVS a Malta | 10% su pensione (accordo UE) | 15% a Malta | 2.500 CHF/anno (su 25k CHF) |
| Nomade digitale a Dubai | 0% (se residenza >183 giorni) | 0% (no tasse su reddito) | 0 CHF |
| Manager distaccato a NY | 20% su 30% dello stipendio (3 anni) | 37% USA (federale) | 18k CHF/anno (su 300k CHF) |
| Imprenditore a Singapore | 15% su dividendi (tassa preventiva) | 17% corporate tax | 7.5k CHF (su 50k CHF utili) | ## Emigrating from Switzerland: Tax Obligations and What to Know Before You Go Before leaving Switzerland, the tax return for the current year must be filed **by March 31** (ordinary deadline for most cantons, including Zurich, Geneva, and Ticino). In Basel City, for example, the deadline is set to April 30, while in Vaud, an automatic extension is applied to June 30 for taxpayers with a fiscal year-end. Omission results in a minimum fine of 200 CHF (Art. 130 LIFD), which can reach 10,000 CHF in case of fraudulent declaration. It is mandatory to appoint a Swiss tax representative (Art. 127 LIFD) or provide a valid address for correspondence. In Geneva, the tax office specifically requires a notarized mandate for the representative, with an average cost of 300–500 CHF. Alternatively, services like *Tax Representation Switzerland* (TRS) offer packages starting from 800 CHF/year to manage tax correspondence. ### Procedure for Transferring Taxes Abroad Cantons apply different rules for settling tax liabilities before departure: - Zurich and Aargau: full payment within 10 days of notification of the amount due. - Vaud and Fribourg: installment payment (max 12 months), but with a 0.5% monthly interest on the remaining debt. - Ticino: obligation to deposit a 5,000 CHF bond if the tax debt exceeds 10,000 CHF. > *"In 2023, 12% of transfers abroad from Zurich registered payment delays, with average penalties of 1,800 CHF for non-payment",* reports the Federal Statistical Office (FSO). Pre-Departure Checklist: 1. Request the exit certificate (*Wegzugsbescheinigung*) from the municipality (cost: 50–150 CHF). 2. Verify the VAT account status (if applicable) on the AFD (Federal Office of Customs and Trade) statement. 3. Close 2nd pillar (LPP) accounts: the advance tax is taxed at 10–20% depending on the canton (e.g., 12% in Bern, 18% in Geneva). 4. Cancel the compulsory health insurance (LAMal) within 3 months of departure, otherwise, premiums will be paid up to 3,000 CHF/year even abroad. ### Risks of Unresolved Tax Debts The Swiss tax debt does not prescribe for real estate or bank accounts opened in the country. Concrete examples: - A property in Zug (value 1.2 million CHF) with 3 years of unpaid property taxes (rate 0.3%) accumulates a debt of 10,800 CHF + interest (5% annually). - An account with UBS containing 200,000 CHF not declared: the AFC (Federal Tax Administration) can issue an audit notice with penalties up to 40% of the capital (Art. 175 LIFD). In case of return, the withholding tax (for foreign workers) is applied retroactively if the debt exceeds 5,000 CHF, with a maximum installment period of 5 years (Art. 219 LIFD). 📊 Comparison of Cantons for Outstanding Taxes: | Canton | Interest Rate for Delinquent Taxes | Penalty for Late Declaration | |---------------|---------------------------|--------------------------------| | Zurich | 0.5% monthly | 200–5,000 CHF | | Geneva | 0.6% monthly | 300–10,000 CHF | | Ticino | 0.4% monthly | 150–8,000 CHF | | Vaud | 0.5% + 20 CHF/month | 250–7,000 CHF | ### Tax Treaties to Avoid Double Taxation Switzerland has signed 98 double taxation agreements (as of 2024), but some exceptions remain: - Dividends from Swiss companies: taxed at 35% withholding tax (reduced to 15% for EU residents with form DA-1). - Real estate capital gains: taxable in Switzerland even after transfer if the sale occurs within 5 years (e.g., sale of a house in Lugano purchased in 2020: taxed at 20% on the profit). - 3rd pillar: the advance tax for emigration is taxed at 10% (vs. 0% for transfers to the EU/AELS with a free movement agreement). ⚠️ Critical Cases: - Italian border residents: Italy taxes Swiss income only if it exceeds 75,000 CHF/year (2020 Swiss-Italian agreement), but Switzerland still applies withholding tax (4.37–11.5% depending on the canton). - Remote workers: A Google Switzerland employee who moves to Lisbon but keeps the Swiss contract pays taxes in Switzerland on the 100% of the income (TF 2C_890/2021 ruling). 💡 Practical Solutions: - Open an escrow account (e.g., with Credit Suisse) to block funds sufficient to cover potential tax debts. - Use the moving procedure (*Umzugsmeldung*) online on [ch.ch](https://www.ch.ch) to update the municipality, AFC, and social insurance simultaneously. - For real estate, consider a trust management (cost: 1–2% of the annual value) to avoid direct taxation. 

## Useful tools for your case
To verify your within/over 20 km tax scenario, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [tax return guide](nav:tax-return). ## What to do in practice
In this context, it is important to have conventions stipulated by Switzerland to avoid double taxation, which regulate which country can levy taxes on which income. Switzerland has concluded such agreements with over 100 countries, including all EU and AELS countries.

### Steps to follow
1. **Submit the tax return**: Before leaving Switzerland, it is essential to submit the tax return for the current year. This allows the local tax office to calculate all the taxes owed.

2. Appoint a representative: It is important to appoint a Swiss domiciled representative or provide a mailing address, depending on what the various tax authorities require.

3. Contact the tax office: It is recommended to contact the tax office at least 30 days before the date of the transfer abroad after consulting the website of the local municipality.

### Useful tools
For further information and to use useful tools for calculating taxes, you can consult the website of the Federal Department of Foreign Affairs (FDFA) and the Organization of Swiss Abroad (OSA).

## In brief ### Scenario of an Independent List
The prospect of the Lega running alone, as feared by Piero Marchesi, calls for a reflection on the political and strategic implications in the Canton of Ticino. If Claudio Zali were to decide to present himself on a different list, the Lega would have to redefine its electoral campaign, focusing on consolidating its own electorate without the support of figures who could attract cross-party votes or votes from specific sectors. This scenario could lead to a greater emphasis on the Lega's core identity and programmatic issues, in an attempt to mobilize its base and clearly differentiate itself from its opponents.

The strategy of an independent list could also result in greater media exposure for the Lega's candidates, who would be forced to take individual responsibility for communicating and promoting their political agenda. Without the protection of a broader electoral agreement, each candidate would have to demonstrate their added value and ability to win popular support. This could translate into a greater organizational and financial effort for the campaign, with the need to activate more extensive territorial networks and make the most of available communication channels, including digital ones, to reach a wider audience.

### Comparison with Past Scenarios
Historically, political alliances in Ticino have often played a decisive role in the outcome of cantonal elections. The possibility that the Lega might run alone, without an agreement with Zali, raises questions about the resilience of certain coalitions or the effectiveness of political strategies based on the sum of different forces. If the original source does not specify previous elections with similar dynamics, it is possible to hypothesize that such a move would represent a significant change from the past. An analysis of previous cantonal political dynamics could reveal whether these divisions have favored or hindered individual political forces in the past. Marchesi's decision could therefore be seen as an attempt to anticipate or manage a potential fragmentation of the political front, seeking to preserve the Lega's strength and influence in an evolving context. The choice to present itself independently, although risky, could also be seen as an affirmation of independence and ideological coherence, elements that sometimes resonate positively with a part of the electorate.

### Implications for the Cantonal Political System
The potential internal division or failed alliance between Marchesi and Zali could have repercussions on the balance of political forces in the Council of State and the Grand Council. If the Lega were to present itself with a single-color list, its ability to elect its representatives would depend entirely on the support obtained by the list itself. This could lead to greater internal competition among candidates from the same political area, but also to a potential loss of seats in favor of other forces that could benefit from the fragmentation of the vote. Ticino's cantonal politics, already characterized by complex dynamics, would face an additional element of uncertainty, with possible cascading effects on government stability and the ability to address the canton's political and economic challenges. The spring, set as the deadline for the decision, will therefore be a crucial period for observing developments and understanding the strategies that will be adopted by the various political actors.

item.title: AVS Pensions Abroad: Conditions and Agreements
item.description: Swiss residents in 21 non-EU/Schengen countries can voluntarily pay AVS contributions. Social conventions guarantee equal treatment.
item.content:encoded:
## In Brief
- Voluntary AVS/AI contributions are possible for residents in 21 non-EU/AELS countries
- Voluntary AVS/AI requires at least 5 consecutive years of contributions in Switzerland
- Social security conventions with 21 countries guarantee equal pension rights

## Key facts
- **What**: Payment of voluntary AVS contributions for residents abroad
- Countries: 21 non-EU/AELS countries with conventions
- Deadline: Application within 12 months after exiting mandatory AVS
- Condition: Swiss or EU/AELS citizenship
- Costs: Voluntary AVS/AI deficit reached CHF 149M by 2000

The Swiss Confederation has signed 21 social security conventions with non-EU/AELS countries. These guarantee equal treatment for involved citizens. Swiss residents in these countries can enroll in voluntary AVS/AI after meeting specific requirements, such as citizenship and a minimum of 5 years of contributions in Switzerland immediately before exiting mandatory AVS. Enrollment numbers dropped from 57'000 (2000) to 11'000 (2021) due to financial reforms.

### How the system works
Conventions stipulate that residents in partner countries can receive partial pensions from EU/AELS states where they worked. Those living abroad can pay voluntary contributions only if:
- Hold Swiss or EU/AELS citizenship
- Made contributions in Switzerland for 5 consecutive years before leaving mandatory AVS
- Submit an application within 12 months of exiting

### Crucial figures
By 2000, the voluntary AVS/AI deficit reached CHF 149M. 73% of mandatory contributors paid above the minimum, while only 50% of volunteers exceeded CHF 378/year.

### Which countries are included?
Among the 21 countries featured:
- Tunisia
- EU/AELS countries are excluded from voluntary payments
- Full list available on DFAE and OSE ### Implications for Foreign Residents
Swiss citizens in non-EU/EFTA countries can maintain ties with the AVS only in **specific cases**. For example, in Latin America (where 25,000 Swiss citizens reside according to FDFA 2023), those who worked in Switzerland for 5+ years (Art. 14 LAVS) can continue voluntary contributions, with a minimum annual payment of CHF 503 (2024). For EU/EFTA citizens like Germans or Norwegians, registration is permitted only if residing outside the area and having paid at least 12 months of mandatory contributions.

⚠️ Exception: Residents in states with bilateral agreements (e.g., USA, Canada) follow different rules.

### Comparison with the Past
Before the 1 January 2001 reform (LF 83a), 120,000 Swiss citizens abroad were enrolled in AVS without contribution requirements. Today:
- Obligation of 5 years of contributions (minimum CHF 25,150 total)
- Application within 12 months of emigration, with a 2% annual penalty on unpaid contributions (Art. 30a OAVS)

📊 CSC data: Enrolments plummeted from 120,000 (2000) to 24,000 (2021), with a 42% drop in Latin America alone.

### How to Calculate the Pension
The official AVS formula considers:
1. Contribution years (max 44)
2. Average annual income (min. CHF 14,100, max. CHF 84,600)
3. Conversion coefficient (6.8% in 2024)

Example: 10 contribution years with average income of CHF 50,000 → Annual pension of CHF 3,400 (CHF 283/month).

💡 DSS online tool: *Foreign AVS calculator* updated with 2024 rates.

### Financial Risks
The Geneva CSC (handling 35% of foreign cases) introduced cross-checks with tax data from 15 countries in 2022. Falsifying declared income incurs fines up to 150% of evaded contributions.

> "18% of applications are rejected due to inconsistencies between actual residence and registry data" (Marc Bourgeois, CSC director).

### Practical Cases
- Scenario A: Maria Schmidt, German, 6 years of work in Zurich (2015-2021), relocates to Tunisia in 2022. Can pay CHF 800/month for 15 years, receiving a supplementary pension of CHF 650/month at age 65.
- Scenario B: Paolo Rossi, Swiss in France, is excluded from voluntary contributions under the 2002 EU-Switzerland Bilateral Agreement unifying social security treatments.

### New Trends
The enrolment collapse (-80%) reflects:
1. Pension reforms in countries like Chile (capitalization system since 2008) and Brazil (INSS extended to expats since 2015)
2. Private fund boom: +30% subscriptions to products like VIAC (Zurich) and Frankly (Geneva) since 2020
3. Swiss restrictions: 5,300 applications rejected in 2023 for non-compliance with minimum contribution period

### Operational Checklist
1. Verify bilateral agreements on the DSS website
2. Calculate contribution years with CSC statements
3. Submit application within 12 months (form E-401)
4. Declare foreign income with translated documentation
5. Evaluate integration with pillar 3a to cover gaps

## Useful planning tools
To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## AVS Pensions Abroad: Conditions and Conventions

Leaving the Swiss mandatory pension scheme (AVS) and the possibility of receiving a pension abroad are crucial aspects for those choosing to relocate overseas. The Federal Department of Foreign Affairs (FDFA) provides a comprehensive overview of applicable conditions and conventions, but it is essential to carefully verify one's personal situation.

## Registration Steps
The first step involves checking eligibility. Consulting the list of countries on the FDFA website ([https://www.dfae.admin.ch/dfae/it/home/suisse/emigrazione/pensioni-esteri.html](https://www.dfae.admin.ch/dfae/it/home/suisse/emigrazione/pensioni-esteri.html)) is essential, as pension access depends on legal residency in the foreign country. Additionally, it is necessary to check the required contribution period in Switzerland for the pension. For example, to access the AVS pension, at least 10 years of contributions are generally required.

## Application Deadlines
The application for an AVS pension abroad must be submitted within 12 months of leaving the Swiss mandatory AVS scheme. This timeframe is crucial to avoid delays in benefit processing.

## Required Documents
To complete the application, proof of citizenship and an AVS/AI contribution certificate must be provided. A practical example: a Swiss citizen relocating to France and leaving AVS after 15 years of contributions may need to submit documents related to Swiss contributions and French residency proof.

## Contacts
The Swiss Abroad Organisation (OSE) and regional compensation offices are key reference points for clarifications and assistance. For instance, the Zurich Compensation Office (KZ) provides detailed information on social conventions and application procedures.

## Payments and Pension Receipt
AVS pension payments abroad are made annually. Pension receipt depends on reaching the AVS retirement age, which varies by birth year. For example, those born in 1964 have a retirement age of 64.

## Recommended Tools
Using the pension calculator ([nav:pension](https://www.osg.admin.ch/calculatrice-pension)) allows estimating future AVS/AI benefits based on contributions and retirement age. The FDFA's complete guide and social conventions on OSE offer additional useful information.

## Additional Resources
The 'Emigration' page on Swissinfo ([https://www.swissinfo.ch/italiano/emigrazione/pensioni-esteri/](https://www.swissinfo.ch/italiano/emigrazione/pensioni-esteri/)) provides FAQs and further clarifications. The Federal Department of Foreign Affairs is available for specific legal inquiries.

## Final Advice
It is crucial to verify one's situation through official channels before relocating abroad. Pension calculations are sensitive to each contribution year and the specific rules of the residence country. A Swiss citizen moving to Spain and leaving AVS after 12 years of contributions might receive a lower pension compared to someone with 15 years. Failure to verify one's situation could lead to delays or even loss of pension rights.

## In brief
- 25,000 AI job offers in 2025
- +9,000 positions compared to the previous year
- 28% of jobs highly exposed to automation
- Higher salaries in healthcare and energy

## Key facts
- **What**: Historic increase in artificial intelligence job offers.
- When: 2025 data, report published on June 15, 2026.
- Where: Switzerland, with significant impact on Ticino and cross-border workers.
- Who: PwC Switzerland, Federal Council, Kuble, Impiegati Svizzera.
- Amount: 25,000 job offers, +9,000 year-on-year.

Artificial intelligence has ceased to be a futuristic promise to become a structural pillar of the Swiss labor market. According to the AI Jobs Barometer by PwC Switzerland, released on June 15, 2026, job offers requiring specific skills in this field reached 25,000 in 2025. This is a level never reached before, marking an increase of approximately 9,000 positions compared to the previous year. Although the share of total job advertisements remains limited, at 1.8%, the trajectory is unmistakable: AI is reshaping the professional landscape far beyond the borders of the technology sector itself.

### The evolution of required skills
'AI changes how careers begin,' noted Adrian Jones, Head of Workforce at PwC Switzerland. The revolution is not just about the automation of routine tasks that once served as training grounds for new hires, shifting focus toward human capabilities such as discernment, adaptation, and leadership already in the early stages of a career. Companies are therefore forced to review their talent development strategies. PwC's global analysis, which examined over a billion job advertisements across twenty-seven countries and territories, highlights that since 2019, professions most exposed to artificial intelligence have seen an average addition of 248 new skills per role, a growth rate much higher than those less affected by the digital transformation.

### Salary premiums and growth sectors
Possessing AI skills translates into concrete advantages on the compensation front. Those who hold these skills can aspire to higher-than-average salaries, with particularly significant premiums in the healthcare and energy sectors. This data confirms that the demand for such skills is expanding to sectors traditionally distant from pure technology, creating new professional niches. For candidates seeking positions in these fields, the prospects for economic growth are therefore tangible and supported by market data. For the approximately 78,500 Italian cross-border workers active in Ticino, the boom in artificial intelligence presents a two‑sided scenario. On one hand, the chronic shortage of qualified talent in Swiss territory clashes with a growing demand for tech‑savvy profiles, offering concrete opportunities in sectors such as healthcare, energy, and finance. On the other hand, the speed at which required skills change poses the risk of rapid professional obsolescence, making continuous training no longer optional but a strategic necessity.

### The information gap on support tools
A Federal Council report on professional reintegration, adopted on 5 June 2026, highlights a specific issue for those living across the border: cross‑border workers are often a less‑informed category regarding Swiss institutional channels. In a rapidly changing labour market, this tool is an essential lever, but knowledge of it remains limited among the cross‑border population. To this is added cantonal variability: availability and access practices for these funds differ from canton to canton, a fragmentation that the federal government itself flags as a critical point to address.

### Exposure of various professional sectors
The impact of AI is not uniform across all professions. An analysis by Zurich‑based consultancy Kuble, carried out with Swiss Employees and published on 16 June 2026 on a sample of three million jobs and 86 occupations, quantifies the phenomenon. More than one in four jobs in Switzerland (28%) is highly exposed to artificial intelligence, while for 34% exposure is medium and for 38% it is low. The sectors most at risk are office‑based: software developers, cybersecurity specialists and database administrators, system administrators, but also workers in administration, graphics, public relations, journalism, translation, and legal and financial consultancy. By contrast, construction and crafts remain almost entirely excluded, while healthcare and the social sector show relative protection, confirming opportunities for those working in these fields. ## In brief
- Salary data of old cross-border workers in tax returns
- Error in data transmitted from Switzerland to Italy
- Unions will seek clarification

- **What**: Automatic transmission of salary data of old cross-border workers
- When: 2026 pre-filled tax returns
- Where: Ticino and Italy
- Who: Italian cross-border workers employed in Ticino
- Amount: Not specified

The concern is high among old Italian cross-border workers in Ticino. Their salary data has appeared in the 2026 pre-filled tax returns of the Italian Revenue Agency. This event is due to the automatic transmission of tax information between Switzerland and Italy, which has included the data of workers hired before July 17, 2023, despite them being subject to a transitional regime of exclusive taxation in Switzerland.

The situation has raised fears among workers, who fear possible subjection to Italian Irpef tax. Giuseppe Augurusa, national secretary of Cgil cross-border workers, stated that unions are working to remove this error and delete the salary data of old cross-border workers from Italian documentation.

## Transmission error

The transmission of salary data occurred through the Common Reporting Standard (CRS), an automatic mechanism for the exchange of tax information developed by the OECD and applied between Switzerland and Italy. Under the new bilateral agreement that came into force in 2023, cantonal tax authorities are required to annually transmit the salary data of cross-border workers to the Italian Revenue Agency. However, the information flow was activated indiscriminately for the entire category, without previously excluding old cross-border workers, who are not subject to Irpef tax reporting obligations in Italy.

The transmitted data includes earned dependent employment income, withholding taxes paid in Switzerland, and employer details. The presence of this data in the pre-filled declaration does not automatically subject income to Italian taxation, nor does it generate a reporting obligation in itself. However, the issue of protecting salary data, considered sensitive, remains open and concerning.

This situation has prompted many workers to turn to unions, which are working to resolve the error and protect the rights of cross-border workers. Contact the union for more clarification on what to do. ## Practical implications

The error in transmitting salary data can have several practical implications for older cross‑border workers. First, it is important that the affected workers contact their unions for clarification and assistance. Unions are working to remove the incorrect data from tax returns and to protect cross‑border workers' rights.

Second, workers must verify their tax situation and ensure that the transmitted data are correct. If errors are found, they need to act promptly to avoid any problems with the Italian Revenue Agency.

## Comparison with the previous situation

Before the error, older Italian cross‑border workers employed in Ticino were not subject to Italian IRPEF filing obligations. The automatic transmission of salary data has changed this, causing concern among workers. The main difference is that now the salary data of older cross‑border workers are included in the pre‑filled Italian tax returns, creating the possibility of being subject to Italian IRPEF.

This situation highlights the importance of proper management of tax information and the protection of personal data. Unions are working to fix the error and ensure that cross‑border workers' rights are respected.

## Possible scenarios

One possible scenario is that the error is resolved quickly and the salary data of older cross‑border workers are removed from the Italian tax returns. In that case, the situation would return to normal and workers could continue to benefit from the transitional regime of exclusive taxation in Switzerland.

However, if the error is not resolved, older cross‑border workers could face tax problems with Italy. In that case, they would need to act promptly to protect their rights and avoid potential penalties.

item.title: Swiss Parliament Approves Partial Funding for 13th AVS Pension
item.description: 0.4% VAT increase approved, wage contributions rejected: only half the 13th AVS pension costs covered
item.content:encoded:
## In brief
- Swiss Parliament approves VAT increase from 8.1% to 8.5%
- Wage contributions not increased, limited financial coverage
- 13th AVS pension will cost about CHF 4.2 billion from December 2026

## Key facts
- **What**: partial funding of the annual 13th AVS pension
- When: parliamentary decision in 2026, first payment December 2026
- Where: Swiss Parliament, Bern
- Who: National Council, Green Liberal Party
- Amount: VAT increase of 0.4 percentage points

The Swiss Parliament has approved a plan for only partial funding of the new annual 13th AVS pension. After intense debates, the National Council approved a 0.4% increase in the value-added tax (VAT), raising the standard rate from 8.1% to 8.5%. The reduced rate for hotels will go up from 3.8% to 4%, while the minimum rate of 2.6% for essential goods such as food and medicine will remain unchanged.

This decision was made possible by a change in position from the Green Liberal Party, which had previously opposed a permanent VAT increase. However, Parliament rejected a proposal to raise wage contributions by 0.2 percentage points, a measure that was part of a compromise between the two chambers.

By excluding this component, the VAT increase will cover only about half of the additional costs related to the 13th pension. The first payment is scheduled for December 2026, with an estimated total cost of about CHF 4.2 billion.

### Immediate implications
The Federal Council had prepared backup plans in case Parliament did not approve any funding, considering a larger VAT increase or a combination of VAT and wage contribution increases. At present, neither chamber appears willing to support these solutions.

Since the VAT increase requires a constitutional amendment, it will be subject to a popular and cantonal referendum, likely in November 2026. Meanwhile, the first two annual payments of the 13th pension will be made without dedicated financial coverage, with an estimated deficit of around CHF 9 billion. Even after the increase takes effect, coverage will remain insufficient, covering less than half of the costs starting in 2028. The partial approval of funding for the 13th AVS has significant practical implications for the Swiss economy and society. The increase in VAT directly affects the cost of living for residents, influencing the price of goods and services, and thus the purchasing power of families.

2. Constitutional referendum: likely scheduled for November 2026, it will involve both citizens and Cantons to approve the VAT increase as a constitutional amendment.
3. Business adjustments: once approved, companies will need to update billing systems and prices to reflect the new VAT rate.
4. 13th AVS payment: the first disbursement is planned for December 2026, advanced without full funding for about two years.

item.title: Too hot to work or sleep: what are your rights
item.description: What the law says about excessive heat at work, school and home

## In brief
- There's no 'heat exemption' at work or school
- Companies must protect employees' health with adequate measures like ventilation and regular breaks
- An overly hot dwelling can be considered a defect from a tenancy law perspective

## Key facts
- **What**: Rights of workers and tenants during the heatwave
- When: Summer 2023
- Where: Switzerland
- Who: Employees, schoolchildren, tenants
- Amount: Not specified

The great heat can make life difficult, especially when you have to work or study. What rights do you have in these situations: at the workplace, at school, or at home? The 'heat exemption' remains a myth: it doesn't exist, even when the thermometer reads over 30 degrees in the shade. By law, companies are required to protect the health of their employees through adequate measures. For example, according to the Ordinance on Accident Prevention of December 19, 1983, companies must ensure a suitable working temperature. In the event of high temperatures, measures such as installing ventilation or cooling systems can be adopted.
> "Companies must take all necessary measures to protect the health of their employees," as established by Article 6 of the Ordinance on Accident Prevention.

In Zurich, for example, some companies have adopted heat adaptation policies, such as the possibility of working from home or having flexible working hours. Tenants, on the other hand, can appeal to tenancy law if their dwelling is too hot due to poor building design or maintenance. In such cases, they can request a rent reduction or improvement works. [object Object]

1. Check the protective measures adopted by the employer, such as the provision of fresh water and the installation of cooling systems. For example, according to the ordinance of the Swiss Federal Council of May 13, 2020, employers must ensure a suitable working temperature.
2. Request more frequent breaks or air conditioning if necessary. In cantons such as Zurich, workers can benefit from specific regulations that provide for longer breaks during heatwaves.
3. Consult the workers' representative or trade union if conditions do not improve. > 'Workers have the right to a safe and healthy working environment' (art. 6, Federal Labour Law, March 13, 1964).

### Procedure for tenants
1. Ventilate the dwelling correctly by opening windows during the cooler hours of the day.
2. Check if the landlord has taken adequate measures to maintain a comfortable temperature, such as installing solar shades or cooling systems. For example, in Geneva, tenants can refer to the specific provisions provided by the Code of Obligations (art. 256a, July 1, 2022).
3. If necessary, contest the situation to the landlord or contact a consumer association such as the Swiss Consumer Federation. A concrete example is the case of a tenant in Bern who received compensation of 1,200 francs for medical expenses incurred due to the excessive temperature in the inadequately cooled apartment.

For more information on your rights and obligations, you can consult the salary calculator or seek information on Swiss laws related to tenancy law, such as the Federal Law on Tenancy (art. 28, January 1, 1990), which provides for compensation for damages resulting from inadequate living conditions.

LUGANO - Caritas Ticino has strengthened its commitment against various forms of poverty, focusing on proximity and relationships as central tools. This emerged from the organization's Annual Assembly, founded in 1942, held last June 16th at the Laudato si’ Center in S. Antonino. The meeting reviewed activities, financial statements, and statutory structure, also offering a reflection on an increasingly complex context.

The most immediate data concerns the volume of work carried out. In 2025, 1,047 people were welcomed into socio-professional integration measures, with a specific composition: 670 unemployed individuals and 377 people in need of assistance. The Social Services opened 358 new cases, a slight increase compared to the 345 of 2024, related to often complex issues. Concurrently, the number of people seeking spaces for meeting and interaction is growing, indicating an increasingly widespread loneliness.

### Activities and Circular Economy

A positive aspect highlighted was the efficiency of circular economy activities. Collection operations yielded significant results: 516,527 kg of used clothing and 1,517,000 kg of electronic devices were recovered. In addition to these materials, hundreds of tons of furniture and objects were processed and reintroduced into the second-hand market. On the agricultural front, the organization produced 93 tons of organic products and processed 748,000 liters of invasive plants on 936,000 square meters.

### 2025 Financial Report

The 2025 financial report concludes with a deficit of CHF 255,682. This represents an improvement compared to 2024, when the deficit was CHF 371,276. Total revenues amount to CHF 9,596,066, compared to costs of CHF 9,851,748. The budget for 2026 forecasts a break-even. Revenues are derived 53% from own activities and 40% from public mandates. The staff, consisting of 82 employees, represents 53% of total costs. In 2025, 10 employees were hired from the integration measures, highlighting the importance of active labor policies in the Ticino social fabric.
 ### Analysis of social and fiscal implications

The strengthening of Caritas Ticino's support network is not merely a matter of social news, but directly affects labor market dynamics and the Swiss social security system. The figure of 670 unemployed women admitted to socio-professional integration measures highlights how active support is crucial for those facing difficult career transitions. These measures, often linked to LPP/BVG regulations, represent a bridge between unemployment and reintegration into the workforce, a central aspect for both cantonal and national economic stability.

item.title: Swiss Pension (LPP) Benefits: Taxation
item.description: Guide to taxing occupational pension (LPP) benefits in Switzerland, focusing on annuities and lump sums.
item.content:encoded:
## In Brief
- Taxation of LPP benefits in Switzerland.
- Difference between capital and annuity taxation.
- Progressive and deductible tax rates.

## Key Facts
- What: Taxation of occupational pension (LPP) benefits.
- When: At the time of withdrawal (capital or annuity).
- Where: In Switzerland, at federal and cantonal levels.
- Who: Workers and pensioners with LPP income.
- Amount: Progressive tax rates, with possible reductions.

Occupational pension provision, commonly known as LPP (Law on Occupational Old Age, Survivors' and Disability Insurance), represents the second pillar of the Swiss pension system. Benefits paid out from this fund, whether in the form of capital or annuity, are subject to taxation. Understanding the taxation methods is crucial for sound financial planning, especially for cross-border workers who fall into certain taxpayer categories. Taxation occurs at the time of withdrawal, whether it's capital or annuity, and distinguishes between direct federal tax and cantonal and municipal taxes. The aim is to ensure adequate tax revenue while maintaining an incentive system for long-term provision. The tax rates applied are progressive, meaning the amount due increases proportionally to the amount of the benefit paid. However, there are deduction mechanisms and relief measures that can reduce the overall tax burden. Swiss legislation provides for separate and favorable taxation of capital benefits compared to ordinary work income or annuity income, recognizing their nature as long-term accumulation and their purpose for wealth building or covering specific post-employment needs. The distinction between annuity and capital taxation is fundamental, as the rates and calculation methods differ significantly, influencing the beneficiary's choice on how to receive their accumulated sums. Federal and cantonal tax authorities collaborate to ensure uniform application of the rules, although significant differences remain between cantons in terms of applicable rates and deductions. It is therefore essential to inquire with the cantonal tax office of residence or tax domicile to understand the specifics applicable to your situation. The transparency of tax rules aims to provide taxpayers with the necessary tools for informed management of their retirement savings. ### Taxation of lump-sum benefits
Capital benefits paid as a lump sum, often chosen at retirement or in the event of an early partial or full withdrawal (for example, to purchase a primary residence or upon leaving Switzerland), are subject to separate and preferential taxation. Federal direct tax is applied at reduced rates compared with the standard rates on ordinary income, and the cantons often follow a similar approach, providing reduced or flat-rate tax rates. These rates are generally progressive, but the effective rate applied is significantly lower than the rate that would apply if the same amount were treated as ordinary income over the course of a year. The taxable base consists of the full amount of the capital withdrawn. It is important to note that, in many cases, the cantons allow a deduction from the taxable base, which may vary as a percentage or as a fixed amount. This tax relief is designed to ease the one-off tax burden, preventing a substantial withdrawal from generating an excessively heavy tax charge in a single tax year. Swiss tax legislation aims to encourage retirement savings, and the preferential taxation of lump-sum benefits is a clear example of this. However, cantonal rules are decisive: rates and deductions vary considerably from one canton to another. For example, some cantons may offer lower rates or more generous deductions than others. For this reason, it is essential to check the regulations in force in your canton of tax residence at the time of withdrawal. The choice between lump-sum benefits and annuities has significant tax implications, and the decision should be made after a careful assessment of the tax and financial scenarios. The possibility of choosing how LPP benefits are paid out is an important lever for optimizing one's post-retirement financial situation, taking into account both liquidity needs and the overall tax impact. Advance planning is key to maximizing the benefits and minimizing the tax burden.

### Taxation of LPP annuities
LPP annuities, meaning the periodic payments the beneficiary receives from retirement onwards, are taxed as ordinary income. This means that they are subject to federal direct tax, cantonal tax and municipal tax, in a manner similar to a salary or other income from dependent employment. The standard progressive tax rates apply to the annual amount of the annuity. Unlike lump-sum benefits, there are no special or reduced tax rates for LPP annuities, as they are considered a continuing stream of income. However, in this case too, the normal tax deductions provided for by law apply. These may include, for example, deductions for medical expenses, contributions to supplementary pension schemes (such as the third pillar), continuing education expenses, or other deductible professional expenses. The taxation of LPP annuities is also influenced by other income received by the retiree, such as the AHV/OASI pension or any income from residual gainful activity. The sum of all these income sources determines the overall tax rate applicable. The beneficiary's tax residence plays a crucial role, as cantonal and municipal taxes vary significantly from one canton to another. Cantons with lower tax rates can offer a significant advantage to retirees. For those residing abroad, taxation follows the provisions of the double taxation convention between Switzerland and the country of residence, as well as the Swiss tax rules applicable to non-residents. It is therefore essential to consult a tax expert to fully understand the implications of the taxation of LPP annuities in relation to one's personal circumstances and place of residence. Pension planning should include an accurate estimate of the taxes payable on LPP annuities, in order to have a clear picture of the available net income.

## Useful planning tools
To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Gestione della tassazione delle prestazioni LPP La gestione della tassazione delle prestazioni LPP richiede un'attenta pianificazione e la conoscenza delle normative vigenti. Innanzitutto, è fondamentale determinare la forma di erogazione più conveniente: capitale o rendita. La scelta dipende da diversi fattori, tra cui l'ammontare della prestazione, la situazione finanziaria personale, le esigenze di liquidità future e, soprattutto, le differenze fiscali tra i cantoni. Per le prestazioni in capitale, è consigliabile informarsi presso l'ufficio delle imposte del proprio cantone di domicilio fiscale per conoscere le aliquote specifiche, le eventuali deduzioni applicabili e le modalità di calcolo. Spesso, i cantoni offrono moduli o guide esplicative per aiutare i contribuenti a compilare correttamente la dichiarazione fiscale. In alcuni casi, potrebbe essere vantaggioso posticipare il prelievo del capitale se la situazione fiscale nell'anno corrente è particolarmente sfavorevole. Per quanto riguarda le rendite, è necessario inserirle nella dichiarazione dei redditi annuale come qualsiasi altro reddito. È importante verificare se la rendita LPP è soggetta a trattenute alla fonte, a seconda della residenza fiscale. Per i lavoratori frontalieri, la situazione può essere più complessa, poiché la tassazione dipende dagli accordi bilaterali e dalle normative fiscali sia della Svizzera sia del paese di residenza. In generale, le rendite LPP percepite da lavoratori frontalieri residenti in Italia sono soggette a tassazione in Italia, ma con la possibilità di dedurre l'importo tassato in Svizzera, secondo la convenzione contro le doppie imposizioni. La consulenza di un esperto fiscale specializzato in fiscalità transfrontaliera è altamente raccomandata per ottimizzare la gestione fiscale delle prestazioni LPP. Per avere una stima preliminare del reddito netto dopo le imposte, è possibile utilizzare strumenti online. Ad esempio, il nostro [calcolatore stipendio](nav:calculator) può fornire indicazioni utili sulla tassazione generale dei redditi in Svizzera, che può essere un punto di partenza per comprendere l'impatto fiscale delle diverse forme di reddito pensionistico. È sempre consigliabile effettuare simulazioni personalizzate e consultare professionisti qualificati per decisioni finanziarie importanti. La previdenza professionale è un pilastro fondamentale del benessere finanziario svizzero, e una corretta gestione della sua tassazione può fare una differenza significativa nel reddito disponibile durante la pensione.

item.title: 15,000 violations in 2025: black labor and wage dumping in Switzerland
item.description: In 2025, SECO detected 15,000 irregularities: construction and hospitality were the hardest-hit sectors. Ticino is among the most active cantons in inspections. Mandatory obligations apply.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief
- Over 15,000 irregularities detected in Switzerland in 2025
- Ticino conducted 2,279 inspections on undeclared work, accounting for 16% of the national total
- 37% of posted companies violate mandatory minimum wages
- 90 employers excluded from public contracts due to serious violations
- 74% of confirmed irregularities concern foreign worker rights

## Key facts
- What: Detection of irregularities in undeclared work and wage dumping
- When: 2025
- Where: Switzerland, with focus on Ticino, Zurich, and Geneva
- Who: State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO), tripartite commissions, cantonal authorities
- Amount: 1,169,509 francs in fines and fees for undeclared work

- What: Violations of foreign worker rights
- When: 2025
- Where: National
- Who: Cantonal authorities
- Amount: 3,493 confirmed cases (+9% compared to 2024)

- What: Underpayment rate in posted companies
- When: 2025
- Where: Switzerland
- Who: Tripartite commissions
- Amount: 37% in sectors with extended collective agreements

- What: Suspected fake self-employment
- When: 2025
- Where: National
- Who: Control authorities
- Amount: 9% of 4,661 inspections

The 2025 inspections revealed a widespread phenomenon of labor market irregularities in Switzerland. The State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO) documented over 15,000 cases of undeclared work, wage dumping, and fake self-employment. Among the most affected sectors, secondary construction, hospitality, and retail emerged as the main areas of violation. Ticino remains one of the most active cantons: with 2,279 inspections on undeclared work, it accounts for 16% of national activity. For wage dumping, the canton is among the top three alongside Zurich and Geneva, with one-third of all national inspections related to accompanying measures. Overall, authorities carried out 14,450 targeted inspections on undeclared work and 38,567 checks under accompanying measures. Fines and fees collected for undeclared work reached 1,169,509 francs. For wage dumping, 1,784 fines and 509 bans on providing services in Switzerland were imposed. Additionally, 90 employers were excluded from public contracts due to serious and repeated violations.

### The role of tripartite commissions
Tripartite commissions, composed of representatives from employers, workers, and authorities, conducted targeted inspections on posted companies. In 21% of cases involving foreign companies temporarily operating in Switzerland, underpayment was detected. Among Swiss companies, the rate dropped to 10%. In sectors with extended collective agreements—such as construction and hospitality—wage violations reached 37%. Parity commissions identified irregularities in 24% of the 4,299 inspections carried out on posted companies. These figures highlight a systematic failure to comply with legal minimum wages, particularly among foreign operators. Violations concern 35% of social insurance law, 33% of foreign worker law, and 32% of withholding tax law. Seventy-four percent of confirmed irregularities relate to foreign worker rights: workers without permits or with invalid permits. Cantonal authorities referred 14,147 suspected cases of undeclared work to specialized agencies. Furthermore, of the 4,661 independent service providers inspected, 9% were found to be engaged in fake self-employment, used to evade insurance obligations and employment regulations. The national relevance of these data is not only statistical: it has a direct impact on those who work, pay taxes and look for a job in Switzerland. Salary dumping not only harms workers, but creates a chain reaction across the whole market. When a foreign company pays 37% less than the contractual minimum wage, it forces Swiss firms to cut costs to stay competitive. This phenomenon undermines the stability of collective agreements, which are the cornerstone of wage protection in Switzerland.

For those living in Ticino or working as cross-border workers, this means the risk of being hired illegally or with fake contracts is higher than commonly believed. Seventy-four percent of confirmed irregularities concern foreigners' rights: workers without a permit or with expired permits. This is not only an immigration issue: it is a social security issue. People working off-the-books do not pay AVS contributions, have no LAMal coverage, and do not accrue pension rights. When a foreign worker is hired illegally, the Swiss pension system loses contributions that will later have to be covered by honest taxpayers.

Ticino, although it has reduced black-labour inspections compared with 2024 (from 2,798 to 2,279), remains a strategic hub. Its geographic position makes it an entry point for many Italian and German second-ment companies. Cantonal authorities therefore play a key role in intercepting these irregularities before they spread to the rest of Switzerland. Yet pressure is rising: with the increase in the cost of living and a shortage of skilled labour, some companies try to cut costs by bypassing the rules.

Another practical implication concerns companies that take part in public procurement. Excluding 90 employers from these contracts is not a symbolic act: it is a concrete deterrent. Anyone who wants to work with the public administration — from cantons to municipalities — must demonstrate compliance with labour regulations. This has a direct impact on small firms operating in construction or cleaning: if they are not compliant, they lose an important market.

Finally, the phenomenon of false independents. Nine percent of the 4,661 inspections revealed fraudulent use of the independent status to evade the obligation to pay AVS and LPP contributions. This is especially common in the transport, home-care and construction sectors. For those working as "freelance" in Switzerland, this means the Federal Authority may verify professional status: if you are not truly autonomous, you risk a sanction and retroactive payment of unpaid contributions.

## Useful planning tools
To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). If you work in Switzerland, particularly in construction, hospitality, or as a service provider, you need to know how to protect yourself and verify your employment status. Here’s what to do concretely: 1. **Check your contract** — Determine whether it’s an employment contract or a service agreement. If you’re required to follow your employer’s schedules, locations, and instructions, you’re an employee, even if you’re called 'self-employed'. 2. Verify your contributions — If you work in Switzerland, your employer must pay AVS and LPP contributions. Check your payslip: there must be entries labeled 'AVS/AHV' and 'LPP/BVG'. If they’re missing, report it to the Cantonal Labour Office. 3. Use the AVS calculator — On Frontaliere Ticino, use the [AVS calculator](nav:pension) to verify whether your contributions are correct. Enter your salary and your canton: the algorithm will tell you if your employer has paid the mandatory 5.05%. 4. Report wage dumping — If your salary is below the collective agreement minimum for your sector, you can report the irregularity via the SECO portal or the Ticino Cantonal Labour Office. You don’t need a lawyer — just a written statement with dates, your contract, and payslips. 5. Check your permit — If you’re a foreign national, confirm that your residence permit is valid and matches your type of work. A G permit does not allow you to work as a self-employed person; a B permit is invalid if not renewed. 6. Keep records of your documents — Save copies of contracts, payslips, and AVS payment receipts. These are your proof in case of an inspection. 2025 has shown that inspections are increasing and penalties are becoming stricter. Don’t wait until you’re caught — act now. If you’re an employer, ensure your employees are hired properly. If you’re a worker, reject any offers that don’t include contributions. The cost of undeclared work isn’t just financial — it’s your future security. To check whether your salary aligns with your sector’s collective agreement, use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator). Enter your sector, canton, and position: the algorithm will show you the legal minimum wage. Don’t let wage dumping steal your rights.

## In brief

- Summer session of Parliament: three key dossiers
- 13th AVS: 0.4% VAT increase

## Key Facts

- **What**: Discussion on three main dossiers: nuclear, 13th AVS, and minimum wages.
- When: Summer session of the Swiss Parliament.
- Where: Bern.
- Who: National Council and Council of States.
- Amount: 0.4 percentage point VAT increase.

With the closure of the summer session of the Federal Assembly in Bern, three major dossiers have been postponed to a popular vote. These concern the opening to nuclear energy, the financing of the 13th AVS, and the issue of minimum wages in collective labor agreements.

The National Council and the Council of States have given the green light to the indirect counterproposal of the Federal Council to the 'Stop Blackout' initiative. With this change, the current ban on building new nuclear power plants in Switzerland is lifted. This represents a strategic shift from the popular vote ten years ago, which decided on the gradual phase-out of nuclear energy.

### Energy dossier: nuclear and VAT

To finance the 13th AVS, the Parliament approved a 0.4 percentage point increase in VAT, without affecting wages. This solution was imposed by the Constitution and will need to be approved in a popular vote. The major AVS 2030 reform, which also includes an increase in the retirement age, will remain on the table for discussion.

### Minimum wages: referendum announced

Regarding minimum wages, the Parliament decided to prioritize those set in collective labor agreements over those established at the cantonal level. The Swiss Trade Union Federation has already announced a referendum, arguing that the law overrides the democratic choices of cantons and municipalities, such as Geneva, Neuchâtel, Zurich, and Ticino, which had introduced minimum wages for all workers. With the new provisions, collective labor agreements will prevail over cantonal laws, directly affecting the lowest wages in sectors such as catering, cleaning, and hairdressing.

### Fireworks: final surprise

In closing the session, the National Council rejected the indirect counterproposal to the popular initiative that sought to ban fireworks. In this case as well, the decision will go to a popular vote. The summer session of the Swiss Parliament has left three major dossiers that will return to the Swiss people. These concern the opening to nuclear power, the financing of the 13th AVS, and the issue of minimum wages in collective contracts.

## In brief
- The Federal Council has put the 'Transport '45' project out for consultation to define the future of Swiss mobility
- ProGottardo criticizes the absence of Ticino in the priorities for the completion of the transalpine axis
- There are no projects for the completion of the transalpine axis, particularly for the access routes to AlpTransit
- Priority given to lines such as Neuchâtel–La Chaux-de-Fonds and Zurich-Stadelhofen with specific investments

## Key facts
- **What**: 'Transport '45' project for Swiss mobility
- When: Consultation until 2027
- Where: Switzerland, with a focus on cantonal diversity
- Who: Federal Council and ProGottardo
- Amount: 2.5 billion francs for 68 projects

The Federal Council has put the 'Transport '45' project out for consultation, which will define the future of mobility in Switzerland and its connections with Europe in 2027. ProGottardo – European Railway criticizes the project's approach, considering it 'short-sighted' and unable to outline a comprehensive perspective for rail infrastructure.
> 'The 'Transport '45' project does not take into account the needs of Ticino and the Alpine regions.'

Ticino is once again excluded from the completion of the transalpine axis with access routes to AlpTransit. For example, the project does not include significant investments to improve the Gotthard route, fundamental for the connection between Zurich and Milan.
Among the priority projects are interventions on lines such as Neuchâtel–La Chaux-de-Fonds, with an investment of 340 million francs, and the upgrade of Zurich-Stadelhofen station. The consultation will conclude in 2027 and includes the implementation of 68 infrastructure projects totaling 2.5 billion francs. The Federal Act on Additional Financing and Guarantee of Public Transport (LFT) of 2022 allocated funds for public transport projects. ### Ticino's Challenges
The ProGottardo highlights that Ticino is facing increasing difficulties related to traffic, environmental impact, and economic and territorial development due to its exclusion from the priority projects planned under the Swiss railway infrastructure development program 'Affari dei trasporti ’45'. The document lists 68 projects with a total value of 2.5 billion CHF and defines the priorities, including the Neuchâtel–La Chaux-de-Fonds line, the expansions of the Geneva and Basel stations, and the second base gallery of the Zimmerberg. However, the southern Alps region is not included in the priorities. For example, the Bellinzona-Lugano railway line, crucial for connecting Ticino with the rest of Switzerland, is not among the priority projects.

### Future Prospects
The ProGottardo criticizes the lack of mention in the 2031 Transport Message of the completion of the north-south axis with access to Ceneri and Gottardo. The association calls for a unified stance from the State Council and the Ticinese Chamber of Deputies to the Federal Assembly to advocate for the needs of the southern Alps. According to the ProGottardo, it is essential that the Canton takes action to protect its interests, as demonstrated in the past with the 2016 Alptransit referendum, which obtained a 57.4% approval rate at the cantonal level. The lack of investments in Ticino's infrastructure risks exacerbating traffic congestion and compromising the CO2 emission reduction targets set by the 2011 CO2 Law, which aims for a 50% reduction by 2030.

> 'Ticino must be a protagonist of its own future, it cannot remain on the margins of Swiss mobility decisions.'

It is essential that the State Council and the Ticino Cantonal Parliament adopt a cohesive position to make the voice of Ticino heard at the federal level.
For example, the Canton of Grisons has already expressed its opposition to reducing the frequency of regional trains, highlighting the importance of **public mobility** for peripheral regions.

item.title: Cross-border unemployment in Switzerland: how it works
item.description: The complete guide to unemployment for cross-border workers in Switzerland: SECO rules, the U1 form, and state-to-state reimbursements.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief
- Unemployment benefit is claimed in the worker's country of residence.
- Switzerland issues the U1 form to certify work periods.
- Cantonal unemployment insurance funds handle the applications.

## Key facts
- What: Cross-border unemployment management
- Who: Workers residing abroad and former Swiss employers
- Entity: SECO and unemployment insurance funds of the cantons
- Document: Community form PD U1
- Rule: EU coordination regulation of social security systems

The loss of a job in Switzerland triggers a specific procedure for workers residing in neighbouring countries. According to the coordination rules of social security systems, the competence to pay full unemployment benefits lies with the worker's country of residence. This means that a citizen residing in Italy, France or Germany who loses employment in Switzerland will not receive unemployment benefits directly from Swiss funds, but from the social security authority of their own country.

However, the entire process relies heavily on the data accumulated during the period of activity in Switzerland. The State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO) coordinates the implementation of these directives at the federal level, ensuring that the cantons and their respective unemployment insurance funds correctly process the necessary data for the transfer of social rights. During the employment relationship, the employee regularly pays unemployment contributions, which are recorded together with other mandatory deductions such as those for old-age provision [AVS/AHV](nav:pension) and for occupational pension provision [LPP/BVG](nav:pension).

### The role of SECO and Swiss funds
SECO ensures that cantonal unemployment insurance funds promptly provide the documentation required by workers to claim their rights abroad. The key document in this context is the PD U1 certificate, which officially records the relevant contribution periods completed in Switzerland. Without this form, the social security authority of the country of residence cannot calculate or pay the entitled benefits, effectively blocking financial support for the unemployed worker. Practical application of cross-border unemployment rules shows substantial differences depending on the nature of the unemployment itself. There is indeed a clear distinction between full unemployment and partial or temporary unemployment. This distinction determines which state is financially and administratively responsible for paying the benefits.

## Partial vs full unemployment
In the case of partial unemployment, for example a reduction in working hours due to the company's economic difficulties (short-time work), competence remains entirely Swiss. In this scenario, the reduced hours are compensated directly by the Swiss unemployment fund chosen by the employer. The employee continues to receive part of their salary through the company, which is then reimbursed by the Swiss state. Conversely, when the employment contract is terminated definitively, one enters the regime of full unemployment. In this situation, the worker must immediately contact the placement offices of their country of residence.

## The cost-of-living gap and financial reimbursements
A central aspect for those in this situation is the amount of the benefits. Since the benefits are calculated and paid by the institution of the country of residence, they follow local rules and ceilings, which often do not reflect the high [cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) in Switzerland or the [minimum wage](nav:calculator) parameters applied in some Swiss cantons. To compensate for this imbalance, European regulations provide for a system of reciprocal reimbursements: Switzerland reimburses the state of residence a portion of the benefits paid to the worker, for a period ranging from three to five months, depending on the length of prior contributions made in Swiss territory. This financial compensation between states serves to balance the contribution burden borne in Switzerland against the benefits paid abroad.

## Useful planning tools
To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). - body3: To ensure a smooth transition and minimize waiting times for benefit receipt, it is essential to follow a precise procedure and respect deadlines set by the authorities of the various countries. Neglecting document collection can cause significant delays in payment disbursement.

## Procedure to request the U1 form
The first concrete step to take as soon as you receive notice of termination of your employment contract is to request the Swiss employer for the employer's certificate (international attestation). This document summarizes the employment details, salaries received, and the reasons for dismissal. Once obtained, the worker must forward it to a Swiss unemployment fund, preferably the one of the canton where the company was based. The Swiss fund will verify the data and issue the PD U1 form.

Simultaneously, the worker must register with the employment services of their country of residence within the timeframes prescribed by local legislation. During the registration interview, the U1 form obtained from Switzerland must be presented. If the issuance of the U1 form experiences delays, it is still advisable to proceed with registration in your country to avoid losing accrual rights, submitting the Swiss documentation as soon as it becomes available.
